name: Agent Execution Graphs
question: Which steps can run at the same time?
summary: Model the agent’s work as a directed acyclic graph of steps with explicit dependencies, instead of a strictly sequential loop. Independent tool calls and sub-agents run in parallel, results join where needed, and the runtime can checkpoint, retry a failed node, or resume without redoing the rest.
useCases: Tasks with several independent lookups or tool calls
Multi-agent systems with sub-agents working side by side
Long workflows that must survive failures and restarts

pending = {n: d for n, d in DEPS.items() if n not in done}
ready = [n for n, d in pending.items() if all(x in done for x in d)]
results = await asyncio.gather(*(run(n) for n in ready))
for n, r in zip(ready, results):
def finish(n):                      # earliest finish time of n
return SECS[n] + max((finish(d) for d in DEPS[n]), default=0)

steps.title: Declare steps and dependencies
steps.text: Write the work as a graph: A fetches the application; B, C and D each need only A; E needs all three. Durations are 1, 3, 2, 4 and 1 s.

steps.title: Find what is ready
steps.text: A node is ready when everything it depends on is done. After A finishes, B, C and D are all ready at once.

steps.title: Fan out, with a cap
steps.text: Start every ready node together. A semaphore caps concurrent calls so a wide fan-out does not trip rate limits.

steps.title: Time out, retry, checkpoint
steps.text: Each node has a timeout and retries with backoff. Finished nodes are checkpointed, so a restart resumes instead of redoing them.

steps.title: Join before the next step
steps.text: E starts only when B, C and D have all returned, and it receives all three results.

steps.title: Find the critical path
steps.text: Total time is set by the longest chain: A, D, E = 1 + 4 + 1 = 6 s, against 11 s in sequence. Only speeding up D would help further.

playgroundGuide.scenario: A loan-underwriting agent runs five steps: A fetches the application (1 s), B checks the credit bureau, C analyses bank statements, D verifies employment, and E makes the decision (1 s). In the basic version B, C and D each need only A. You can run the steps in sequence or as an execution graph, and see what happens with a hidden dependency and a failure.
controls: Switch between sequential execution and a graph that runs independent steps in parallel.
Drag the durations of B, C and D, and say whether C needs B’s credit score.
Make D fail once, and choose whether finished steps are checkpointed.

outputs.meaning: Total ÷ the sequential time with no failures.

outputs.name: Critical path
outputs.meaning: The chain of steps that sets the total.

outputs.name: Result correct
outputs.meaning: False when a step reads data that is not ready yet.

presets.name: Sequential
presets.expect: Every step waits for the previous one: 1 + 3 + 2 + 4 + 1 = 11 s.

presets.name: Execution graph
presets.expect: B, C and D run together after A: 1 + 4 + 1 = 6 s, a 1.83× speed-up. The critical path is A → D → E.

presets.name: Hidden dependency
presets.expect: C really needs B’s credit score, but the graph does not say so. Still 6 s, but the result is wrong.

presets.name: Failure, no checkpoints
presets.expect: D fails once and the whole workflow restarts from A: 5 s lost, 11 s in total. With checkpoints it would be 10 s.

missions.text: Finish in 6 s or less with a correct result.
missions.hint: Run in parallel with independent steps, or declare the dependency and shorten B and C.

missions.text: Declare that C needs B, and make B → C the critical path with a correct result.
missions.hint: After declaring it, B and C run in series; make B + C longer than D.

missions.text: D fails once: with checkpoints on, finish in under 9 s.
missions.hint: A retried D takes twice as long, so D itself must get shorter.

numericDrill.question: A takes 1 s, then B (3 s), C (2 s) and D (4 s) can run in parallel, then E takes 1 s. What's the total time with an execution graph, in seconds?
numericDrill.answer: Sequential: 1 + 3 + 2 + 4 + 1 = 11 s. Graph: 1 + max(3, 2, 4) + 1 = 6 s. D is on the critical path, so speeding up B or C changes nothing.

interview.question: What is the critical path in an agent workflow?
interview.answer: The longest chain of dependent steps. It sets the minimum end-to-end time, so speeding up steps off the critical path doesn't reduce total latency.

interview.question: How do you handle a failed branch in a parallel graph?
interview.answer: Give each node its own timeout and retry policy, checkpoint completed nodes so retries don't rerun them, and decide per join whether to continue with partial results or fail.

mistakes.fix: Make dependencies explicit and merge results with reducers
Cap concurrency to respect rate limits

quiz.question: A trip agent searches flights (3 s), hotels (4 s) and visa rules (2 s), which are independent, then builds the itinerary (1 s). How long does it take as a graph?
quiz.explanation: max(3, 4, 2) + 1 = 5 s, against 10 s in sequence.

quiz.question: What is the critical path of an agent workflow?
options: The longest chain of dependent steps, which sets the minimum total time
The step with the most tool calls
The step most likely to fail
quiz.explanation: Only shortening the critical path reduces total latency.

quiz.question: What should every node in an agent graph have? Select all that apply.
quiz.explanation: Explicit inputs, timeouts and retries make parallel execution safe and resumable.

quiz.question: After fanning out 50 product lookups at once, many fail with HTTP 429. What is the fix?
options: Cap concurrency, for example with a semaphore, and back off on 429s
quiz.explanation: Parallelism multiplies the request rate; respect the API’s limits.

quiz.question: A takes 2 s; B (5 s) and C (3 s) both need only A; D needs B and C and takes 1 s. Which change reduces total time?
options: Speed up nothing: it is already optimal
quiz.explanation: Total = 2 + max(5, 3) + 1 = 8 s. B is on the critical path; C is not.

quiz.question: In a parallel graph, the fraud-score step sometimes reads an empty account profile. What is the likely cause?
options: A hidden dependency: it needs the profile step’s output but the graph does not say so
quiz.explanation: Declare the dependency so the runtime orders the steps.

quiz.question: A 9-step claims workflow fails at step 7 and restarts from step 1 every time. What would help most?
options: Checkpoint finished steps so a retry resumes at step 7
quiz.explanation: Checkpoints turn a full rerun into a retry of the failed node.

quiz.question: In LangGraph, g.add_edge(["credit", "statements", "employment"], "decide") does what?
options: Runs “decide” after all three nodes have finished
Runs the three nodes in sequence
quiz.explanation: A list of sources creates a join that waits for all of them.

quiz.question: Which are good candidates for parallel execution? Select all that apply.
options: Independent sub-questions of a research task
Two steps that update the same record
quiz.explanation: Steps that write the same state conflict; they need ordering.

quiz.question: An agent makes 5 independent API calls of 1.5 s each, then a 0.5 s summary. How long does it take with all calls in parallel?
What does LLMCompiler do?
options: Plans function calls as a dependency graph and executes independent ones in parallel
quiz.explanation: A planner produces a DAG of calls that an executor runs concurrently.

quiz.question: A model API returns three tool calls in one response (parallel tool use). What should the application do?
options: Execute them concurrently and return all results together
Ask the model to choose one
quiz.explanation: The model has signalled they are independent, so run them at the same time.

quiz.question: A prior-authorization workflow must wait up to three days for a doctor’s approval and survive deployments meanwhile. What fits best?
options: Durable execution with checkpoints, such as Temporal or a checkpointed LangGraph run
quiz.explanation: Long waits need state that survives restarts.

quiz.question: What are the risks of parallelizing an agent’s tool calls? Select all that apply.
options: Hitting rate limits all at once
quiz.explanation: The risks are real but manageable; parallelism does not guarantee errors.

quiz.question: Four independent bank API calls take 3 s each, and a semaphore allows 2 at a time. How long do they take?
quiz.explanation: Two waves of two calls: 2 × 3 = 6 s.

quiz.question: Tasks vary so much that no fixed graph fits them. What is a good approach?
options: Force one static graph on every task
Let a planner build a graph per task, then execute it
quiz.explanation: Dynamic planning keeps parallelism without a rigid structure.

quiz.question: One of three optional enrichment calls times out before the join. What should the join do?
options: Decide per join: for an optional input, continue with partial results and record the gap
Retry the whole workflow from the start
quiz.explanation: Required and optional inputs deserve different policies.

quiz.question: A workflow takes 11 s sequentially and 6 s as a graph. What is the speed-up?
Which help you decide what to optimize in an agent workflow? Select all that apply.
options: Trace spans with each node’s duration
The average duration of all nodes
A timeline (Gantt) view of the run
quiz.explanation: Averages hide which chain sets the total; traces and the critical path show it.

quiz.question: What should checkpointing let you do? Select all that apply.
options: Resume after a crash without rerunning finished nodes
Retry only the node that failed
Inspect the state at each step when debugging
quiz.explanation: Checkpoints store completed work and state; they are not a reason to skip checks.
